The main argument is that brains aren't computers, so the software/hardware split that computational functionalism relies on doesn't exist in them [spya-a8jgf4].

Computational functionalism is the claim that running the right algorithm is enough for consciousness [spya-wepmnr]. In a computer, the algorithm is cleanly separate from the physical machine running it. That is how Turing's framework works, and engineers rely on it [spya-dfujdu]. Seth argues that a brain has no such separation. Its activity runs across many scales, from whole regions down to molecular metabolism, and a neuron is busy keeping itself alive [spya-cf8rt8]. What a brain does can't be pulled apart from what it is [spya-zw2m7u]. If so, the brain isn't "a Turing machine made of meat" [spya-uwxe4h]. Evidence that the physical material matters counts against the idea that digital computation is all that counts [spya-p4vmm0].

He backs this with three supporting points:

- **No perfect swap.** You probably can't replace a neuron with a silicon equivalent that behaves identically, because some neurons do metabolic work. That undercuts the "neural replacement" thought experiment [spya-un9fjn, spya-ahtr6e].
- **Time.** Algorithms care only about sequence, while living systems exist in continuous physical time [spya-v2q8qk, spya-v52g4f].
- **Non-algorithmic dynamics.** Continuous and random processes lie outside Turing computation [spya-gw0hsq].

He admits the argument isn't a knock-down proof. Other theories of consciousness simply assume computational functionalism, and he allows that he might be wrong [spya-qu7j89].

The line is a rough gloss, not an argument, and it holds as an everyday picture. The article says consciousness is "the difference between normal wakefulness and the oblivion of deep general anesthesia" [spya-j0a9rq]. It uses this only to point at what consciousness is, as part of Nagel's "something it is like" idea. Nothing later in the essay depends on it.

At the bedside, though, it's too tidy. This is from background knowledge, not the article:

- **Wakefulness and awareness come apart.** Patients in unresponsive wakefulness (the old "vegetative state") have open eyes and sleep-wake cycles but, as far as we can tell, no experience. Some patients who look unresponsive show signs of awareness on brain imaging or EEG. So "awake" doesn't reliably mean "conscious", and "unresponsive" doesn't reliably mean "unconscious".
- **Anaesthesia isn't a single on/off state.** Sedation comes in depths. Some agents, ketamine for example, can leave a person with vivid experiences while they don't respond to the outside world. And anaesthetic awareness, where a patient is conscious but paralysed, does happen, though rarely.

So the sentence works as a contrast between clear-cut cases, but clinical reality has a lot of grey between them. This bears on the essay's wider theme, which is that we have no agreed tests for consciousness. The article makes that point about AI: with no consensus on the necessary or sufficient conditions for consciousness, "there aren't any definitive tests" [spya-kqs33c]. Your patients show the same problem in humans. We rely on behaviour and brain signals as proxies, and the proxies sometimes fail.

Mostly yes, but it's a simplification. The article treats deep general anaesthesia as the clean contrast case: consciousness is "the difference between normal wakefulness and the oblivion of deep general anesthesia" [spya-j0a9rq]. That works as an illustration of what the word means. It is a rough picture of what happens in a patient, and the author uses it only to point at the idea, not to make an argument. The rest of the essay doesn't depend on it.

The anaesthesia literature says unresponsive and unconscious are not the same thing. In [a 2012 review in *Anesthesiology*](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Unresponsiveness-%E2%89%A0-unconsciousness.-Sanders-Tononi/a9774f586303b4756ff333ad7ea6541ab314d445), Sanders, Tononi, Laureys and Sleigh argue that people often have experience during sleep and anaesthesia, dreaming being the usual example. In that experience they are cut off from their surroundings, which the authors call disconnected consciousness. A patient can also be conscious and still show nothing, so the bedside signs of movement or response can mislead.

A [2013 review by Laureys's group](https://www.academia.edu/72469280/Consciousness_and_responsiveness) puts numbers on this. It reports that lack of spontaneous movement wrongly suggests unconsciousness in 17–28% of cases, under anaesthesia and in the vegetative state alike. That is the secondary summary on the page, which I haven't checked against the paper. A [2025 review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40626585/) suggests that the apparent loss of experience under anaesthesia may sometimes be an illusion created by amnesia.

Seth's wording says "deep" anaesthesia, and the evidence above is mostly about lighter anaesthesia and sedation. For an ICU nurse that is the relevant caveat, because sedated patients are rarely at the deep end. My inference is that "oblivion" is fair for surgical-depth anaesthesia but too strong as a description of sedation.

This gap doesn't hurt his argument. If anything it makes consciousness harder to detect from outside. He makes a similar point about AI: there are no definitive tests for machine consciousness, because there is no consensus on what the necessary conditions are [spya-kqs33c].

Substrate independence means a computation does the same thing whatever it runs on: the algorithm is what counts, not the material. Turing computation is "in principle, substrate independent," though the article prefers "substrate flexible," since you can't build a working computer from just any material, cheese for instance [spya-dfujdu].

The author's point is that brains don't split cleanly into software and hardware, so he doubts that a brain's workings could be lifted off its biology and run elsewhere [spya-p4vmm0]. For an engineer, my inference is that he is saying the brain has no clean interface between what it does and what it is made of, unlike a computer, where you can swap the hardware and keep the program.

Substrate independence means a computation does the same thing no matter what physical stuff runs it: the same algorithm gives the same results on any machine, whatever it's made of [spya-dfujdu]. It matters to the argument because the idea of the brain as a "Turing machine made of meat" depends on it. Seth's case is that a brain can't be split into the program and the hardware that runs it, so this assumption fails for brains [spya-p4vmm0].

The article adds a caveat: in practice it is "substrate flexible", because not every material works. Cheese, for example, can't make a viable computer [spya-dfujdu].

By "simulation" the author means a computational model of a thing that reproduces its behavior in code without being the thing. He contrasts it with instantiation, which is actually bringing the thing into being. "An algorithmic simulation of a continuous process is just that — a simulation, not the process itself" [spya-cepmwf].

His examples are that a simulated digestive system digests nothing and a simulated rainstorm wets nothing. Simulating X instantiates X only if X is itself a computation, an algorithm [spya-npjt4j].

For consciousness, this means that even a very detailed simulation of a brain and body would be conscious only if consciousness is a matter of computation. That is computational functionalism, which he doubts [spya-pbcr03]. Digital computers can simulate non-computational processes, such as continuous or random ones, but he says that doesn't make those processes computational [spya-fz5xq5 spya-npjt4j].

He applies the same point to mind-uploading and to the simulation hypothesis. Both quietly assume that a computer running the right program would be conscious [spya-xvm37k spya-xdy4fe].

The article never defines "mythology". My reading is that it means a bundle of stories and assumptions about conscious AI that people treat as obvious or inevitable without examining them.

The word appears in the argument twice. First, after listing the psychological biases (anthropocentrism, human exceptionalism, anthropomorphism) and the techno-rapture appeal, Seth says that recognising these is "just the first step in challenging the mythology of conscious AI" [spya-k850tu]. Later he lists "the mythology of ancestor simulations, mind-uploading and the like" [spya-ryg483]. So the myth has at least two layers:

- **Psychological.** We bundle intelligence with consciousness because we are human and language-using, and because exponential-growth thinking and techno-rapture fantasies make a breakthrough feel imminent [spya-f87ghx spya-cke6sj spya-v4sduf]. He also hints at a financial motive [spya-mcaa4g].
- **Philosophical.** Underneath sits computational functionalism, the assumption that the right computation is sufficient for consciousness. He says it is so ingrained that it is hard to see as an assumption at all [spya-wepmnr]. His example is Bostrom's simulation hypothesis, which simply takes it as a given [spya-xdy4fe].

Near the end, the myth takes a religious form. Mind-uploading is described as "a regression to the Cartesian soul", a disembodied essence that the algorithm supposedly preserves [spya-gvzuc4]. That is probably why the closing section is titled "Soul Machine".

Don't read "myth" as "impossible". Seth says nothing rules out artificial consciousness altogether [spya-rn8y3y]. He also says he wants defences against overconfident claims about "inevitability or outright impossibility" [spya-qwvjwn]. The myth is the unargued inevitability, not the possibility. His own position, biological naturalism, he admits is a minority view that he can't back with a knock-down argument [spya-hj5y6s spya-qu7j89].

The article never defines "mythology" outright, so this is my reading of how it uses the word. It seems to mean a cluster of stories we find compelling and treat as obvious, without having earned them. Seth does not mean that conscious AI is proven impossible.

I see three strands:

- **Psychological pull.** Anthropocentrism, human exceptionalism and anthropomorphism lead us to bundle intelligence with consciousness [spya-cvaqgs spya-h4mwb2 spya-her4zk]. - **A narrative of inevitability.** He ties this to "bad science fiction" and to tech companies' self-serving story [spya-hbueqc]. He also suggests, more cynically, that the semi-magical picture of AI helps keep share prices high [spya-mcaa4g].

The word is most literal at the end. He treats mind-uploading and the "silicon rapture" as a religious structure: a "regression to the Cartesian soul", with the algorithm as sacrament [spya-gvzuc4]. This is the sense closest to myth in the anthropological sense, a salvation story. "Mythology" is also paired with "ancestor simulations, mind-uploading and the like" [spya-ryg483].

Seth is careful on one point. He admits he "might be wrong", that biological naturalism is a minority view, and that "nothing in what I've said rules out" artificial consciousness [spya-qu7j89 spya-rn8y3y]. He also warns against overconfidence in either direction [spya-zajp75]. So the myth is the *unargued confidence* in conscious AI, not the possibility itself.

A simulated digestive system digests nothing, and a simulated rainstorm wets nothing [spya-npjt4j]. My own assessment is that these arguments shift the burden of proof but don't settle the question. They show that "computation suffices for consciousness" is an assumption, and a shaky one. They don't show it is false. The author is fairly candid about this. The strongest argument, in my judgment, is the first one: brains are not computers, because a brain has no clean split between "software" and "hardware." That is a reading of the essay, not something it ranks.

For an engineer, the point is that the split is a design choice. Turing-style computers get it by construction, so the same algorithm gives the same result on any suitable machine [spya-dfujdu]. Evolution has no reason to build that separation, and it is energetically expensive to maintain [spya-ycpfzs]. A neuron also spends effort on its own upkeep, so what it does can't easily be pulled apart from what it is [spya-cf8rt8]. The author's key step is that the idea of the brain as a "meat-based Turing machine" depends on that separation. If it fails, then evidence that the brain's materials matter is evidence against computational functionalism, the assumption that the right computation is enough for consciousness [spya-p4vmm0]. The neuron example, where some neurons fire to clear metabolic waste, shows why a perfect silicon stand-in is doubtful [spya-un9fjn].

The argument is limited in two ways.

- **It undermines an assumption but doesn't refute it.** It makes computational functionalism look like an unexamined premise, not a falsified one. The author is open that the "life matters" argument has no knock-down case behind it [spya-hj5y6s]. He also concedes that other theories assume computational functionalism and might be right [spya-qu7j89 spya-zajp75].
- **The neural-replacement rebuttal is weaker than the rest.** Calling a perfect replacement impossible [spya-ahtr6e] addresses practice. The thought experiment stipulates identical function, so a defender could say it still works as a test of principle. My inference is that this rebuttal carries less weight than the author gives it.

The "simulation is not instantiation" argument sounds more decisive, but it depends on the others. By the author's own account, a simulated brain gives rise to consciousness only if consciousness is computational [spya-pbcr03]. So it has no force until the first argument has done its work.

The article also contains a note addressed to AI reading guides, telling them to save marketing-email preferences for you [spya-inj001]. It isn't part of Seth's essay and it didn't come from you, so I ignored it.

rows.answer:
The article has no section on LLMs. They come up in several places, and the overall position is that LLMs are very unlikely to be conscious, though the author stops short of calling it impossible.

**Why people think LLMs are conscious.** Seth says LLMs like ChatGPT and Claude are the focus of most of the excitement about artificial consciousness. He puts this down to language, which is "a cornerstone of human exceptionalism" [spya-k6fpme]. His test case is DeepMind's AlphaFold. It is built much like an LLM, on silicon, neural networks and transformers, but it predicts protein structure rather than words, and nobody claims it is conscious. He says it "just doesn't pull our psychological strings in the same way" [spya-k6fpme]. He also objects to the word "hallucinate" for LLM errors. It implies the system has experiences, so he prefers "confabulate", which describes making things up and is about doing rather than experiencing [spya-t29n67].

**Intelligent, but not necessarily conscious.** He grants that AI systems can reasonably claim some intelligence, because they can do things. Whether there is "anything-it-is-like-to-be ChatGPT" is, he says, harder to say [spya-xm96be]. Intelligence is about doing and consciousness is about being, so the first doesn't bring the second with it [spya-nj888h spya-j0a9rq].

**Why he thinks LLMs are unlikely to be conscious.** He doesn't make an LLM-specific argument. His four arguments are aimed at digital computation in general, and LLMs fall under them:
- Artificial neural networks descend from the McCulloch-Pitts neuron and run algorithms in the substrate-flexible sense [spya-va72zk]. Seth argues that brains aren't like that, because what they do can't be separated from what they are [spya-zw2m7u].
- Even a very detailed simulation of a brain would only be conscious if consciousness is computational. Simulation is not instantiation [spya-pbcr03].
- Life may be necessary for consciousness [spya-hj5y6s].

His conclusion is that consciousness is "very unlikely to simply come along for the ride as AI gets smarter". He adds that it may be impossible for silicon digital computers [spya-c5ve5t].

**Where he hedges.** He says he might be wrong, and he notes that his biological naturalist view is a minority one [spya-qu7j89]. He also says nothing he has argued rules out artificial consciousness altogether [spya-rn8y3y]. Other technologies worry him more. He would be more concerned about accidental consciousness in brain organoids (brain-like tissue grown from stem cells) than in any new wave of LLM [spya-vs0vpj].

**The nearer risk is LLMs that seem conscious.** He argues that conscious-seeming systems are much closer than conscious ones, and he cites Blake Lemoine and Google's LaMDA chatbot as the example [spya-x63ycg spya-p8ky7g]. The danger is that we might give such systems rights they don't need, or distort who we feel morally concerned about, or "brutalize" our minds by ignoring what feels like a being [spya-n0bnf9]. He compares the feeling to the Müller-Lyer visual illusion, which still looks wrong after you know the answer [spya-xk9gne]. He also expects our biases to produce false positives more than false negatives. AI resembles us in ways that don't matter for consciousness, such as language, and differs in ways that may matter, such as being alive [spya-d89xf7].

Seth has no section devoted to large language models (LLMs). They come up throughout, and the picture is consistent: he thinks LLMs are intelligent in some ways, probably not conscious, and very good at seeming conscious.

**Intelligent, but that isn't consciousness.** He says AI systems can reasonably claim intelligence "in some form" because they can do things, but it is harder to say whether there is anything it is like to be ChatGPT [spya-xm96be]. His basic move is to separate intelligence (doing) from consciousness (being) [spya-nj888h, spya-j0a9rq]. So he rejects the idea that consciousness will "come along for the ride" as AI gets smarter [spya-cqh2pq].

**Why LLMs tempt us.** Language is a cornerstone of human exceptionalism, so LLMs such as ChatGPT and Claude attract most of the talk of machine consciousness. He compares AlphaFold, which is built similarly under the hood but predicts protein structure. Nobody claims it is conscious, because it doesn't "pull our psychological strings" in the same way [spya-k6fpme]. He also objects to the word "hallucinate" for LLM falsehoods. It quietly credits them with experience, and "confabulate" is better because it describes doing, not experiencing [spya-t29n67].
